Every year, somebody in the sales team asks me the same question: can I take this client to dinner? And every year my answer is the same: yes, probably. Hospitality is a normal part of business. But before you book the table, ask yourself three questions. First, who is the guest? If the guest works for a government, or for a company the government owns, you are dealing with a foreign official, and the rules are much stricter. Second, is there a decision pending? Under no circumstances should you invite an official who is deciding on your contract next week. Third, would you be comfortable if the bill appeared in the newspaper tomorrow? If the answer to that one is no, the dinner is too lavish. Only when you can answer all three questions calmly should you pick up the phone and book the restaurant. And please, keep the receipt.

Three years ago, our internal audit found a problem in our new office in Texas. A local agent we had hired to help with permits had received a success fee that was much higher than the market rate, and nobody could explain what services he had actually provided. Never had I been in such a difficult meeting with the board. Some people wanted to deal with it internally and say nothing. I argued that we should investigate properly and self-report. Not only was it the right thing to do, it was also the smart thing to do, because the authorities usually treat companies that come forward better than companies that get caught. We terminated the contract with the agent, we hired outside counsel, and we reported what we had found. The investigation took almost a year. In the end, we paid no fine, but we did change the way we check every intermediary.

First, the US sales manager asks Pedro if he can invite an official from a state agency to a steakhouse. Then Pedro checks the policy and sees that a decision on the agency's contract is pending. Next, he explains that under no circumstances can the company host an official while a decision is pending. After the decision is made, the manager suggests a working lunch at the office instead. Finally, Pedro approves the lunch and asks the manager to keep the receipt.
